flashcards.question: What is TRAFFIC (transport) and what is a TRAFFIC (transport) SYSTEM?
flashcards.answer:
• TRAFFIC / TRANSPORT = the purposeful movement of people, goods and information (messages) from one place to another, overcoming spatial distance.
• TRAFFIC SYSTEM = the organised whole of all elements that make transport possible: the transport infrastructure, the means of transport (vehicles), and the people and rules that operate them — across all transport branches (road, rail, water, air).
flashcards.explanation: Transport exists to bridge the gap between where a need arises and where it can be satisfied — in tourism, between the emitting (demand) market and the receptive destination.

flashcards.question: What is a TRAFFIC (transport) MODE / BRANCH? List the basic ones.
flashcards.answer:
A transport mode (branch/sector) is a distinct technical-technological system of transport defined by the medium it uses and its means of transport.

The basic modes:
• ROAD (land)
• RAIL (land)
• WATER — maritime + inland waterway (river-lake-canal)
• AIR
(+ special: pipeline, cable/funicular, etc.)
flashcards.explanation: Each mode has its own infrastructure, vehicles and cost structure, giving it specific advantages and limitations for tourism.

flashcards.question: What is a TRAFFIC (transport) SERVICE, and why is it intangible?
flashcards.answer:
A transport service is the act of moving passengers (or goods) — the 'product' the transport sector sells.

Like all services it is:
• INTANGIBLE — cannot be touched/stored,
• produced and consumed SIMULTANEOUSLY (you 'consume' the trip as it happens),
• cannot be stocked — an empty seat on a departed vehicle is lost forever (perishability).
flashcards.explanation: Because capacity cannot be stored, achieving high capacity occupancy on every departure is the central economic problem of every carrier.

flashcards.question: Distinguish traffic (transport) DEMAND from traffic (transport) SUPPLY (offer).
flashcards.answer:
• TRANSPORT DEMAND = the need for movement — the quantity of transport services users want, where, when and at what price. It is largely a DERIVED demand (people travel to satisfy another need: work, holiday, business).
• TRANSPORT SUPPLY (offer) = the capacity carriers put on the market: routes, frequencies, vehicle capacity, quality and price.
flashcards.explanation: Tourist transport demand is highly SEASONAL and directional, which makes balancing it with a relatively fixed supply difficult and expensive.

flashcards.question: What is meant by the TRAFFIC EFFECT(S) of transport?
flashcards.explanation: In tourism the positive effect (accessibility of destinations) is decisive — but the negative external effects (pollution, congestion) are exactly what transport policy now tries to reduce.

flashcards.question: What is TRAFFIC (transport) POLICY?
flashcards.answer:
Transport policy = the set of goals, measures and instruments by which the state (or the EU) steers the development and operation of the transport system — e.g. building infrastructure, regulating safety, taxes and subsidies, environmental standards, modal-shift incentives.

It is a component of overall economic/development policy; the transport (development) STRATEGY is its long-term plan.
flashcards.explanation: EU transport policy today pushes a modal shift from road/air toward rail and sustainable modes (Green Deal) — see K2 'Future of transport'.

flashcards.question: Why is transport INFRASTRUCTURE economically special (common features of all branches)?
flashcards.answer:
Transport infrastructure (roads, rails, ports, airports) typically requires:
• very LARGE investment,
• a LONG construction period,
• a LONG service life,
• accurate capacity sizing with reserve for peaks,
• as a rule it is built/financed by the STATE (public good), and a one-off user fee rarely covers real costs.
flashcards.explanation: These features explain why infrastructure decisions are strategic, state-led and slow to change — and why capacity bottlenecks persist.

flashcards.question: What does INELASTICITY of a transport branch mean?
flashcards.answer:
Inelasticity = the transport process is tied (functionally bound) to a fixed infrastructure and a line/public organisation, so it cannot freely adapt to an individual user's wishes.

Rail, air and water are relatively INELASTIC (bound to lines, ports, airports, schedules); ROAD transport is the most ELASTIC (door-to-door, individual, flexible).
flashcards.explanation: Inelastic modes usually need another (road) mode to complete the 'door-to-door' chain — a key reason transport in tourism is typically MULTIMODAL.

learn.title: Theoretical Basis of Traffic
learn.content:
What transport is — and why it matters for tourism

Transport (traffic) is the purposeful movement of people, goods and information across space. In tourism it performs the decisive job of connecting the emitting (demand) market with the receptive destination: without accessible, affordable transport there is no tourism at the destination.

Transport SYSTEM = infrastructure + means of transport (vehicles) + people & rules
Basic MODES: ROAD · RAIL · WATER (maritime + inland) · AIR

Key theoretical notions

  • Transport service — intangible, produced & consumed simultaneously, perishable (an empty seat on a departed vehicle is lost forever).
  • Transport demand — a derived, highly seasonal and directional need for movement.
  • Transport supply (offer) — routes, frequencies, capacity, quality and price the carriers put on the market.
  • Traffic effects — economic, spatial and social benefits, but also negative external effects (emissions, noise, congestion, accidents).
  • Transport policy — how the state/EU steers the system (infrastructure, safety, taxes/subsidies, environmental standards, modal shift).

Elastic vs inelastic modes

Road transport is the most elastic (individual, flexible, door-to-door). Rail, air and water are relatively inelastic — tied to lines, ports and airports and to public/line organisation — so they usually need road transport to finish the "door-to-door" journey. This is why tourist transport is typically multimodal.

Why infrastructure is special

All transport infrastructure shares the same economics: large investment, long construction, long service life, careful capacity sizing, and as a rule it is built and financed by the state, because a single user fee rarely covers its true cost. That is why infrastructure is a strategic, slow-moving, policy-driven matter.

flashcards.question: In what TWO basic roles does transport appear in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
1. As a CONNECTOR between the demand (emitting) market and the destination — it makes the destination accessible (the precondition for tourism).
2. As a PART OF THE TOURISM PRODUCT itself — when the trip/ride is the attraction (cruises, panoramic trains, scenic bus tours, nautical tourism).
flashcards.explanation: These two roles structure the whole course: weeks 4–9 always treat each mode 'between markets' (connector) AND 'as a tourism product'.

flashcards.question: Why is the relationship between transport and tourism called INTERDEPENDENCE (two-way)?
flashcards.answer:
Because each drives the other:
• Transport ENABLES tourism — new/cheaper transport (railways, low-cost air) opens new destinations and grows tourist flows.
• Tourism STIMULATES transport — strong tourist demand justifies new routes, capacity, airports, marinas and investment.
flashcards.explanation: Historically, every leap in transport (rail in the 19th c., mass air/charter in the 20th c., low-cost carriers today) triggered a leap in tourism.

flashcards.question: How does transport ACCESSIBILITY shape a destination's tourism?
flashcards.explanation: Low-cost carriers choosing a small regional airport can literally 'put a destination on the map' (see Air transport, K2).

flashcards.question: What is the role of transport COST in the price of the tourism product?
flashcards.explanation: This is exactly learning outcome 3 of the syllabus — recognising the transport cost inside the tourism-product price (developed in week 10, K2).

flashcards.question: Why is tourist transport demand a PROBLEM for carriers (seasonality & direction)?
flashcards.answer:
Tourist demand is:
• strongly SEASONAL (peaks in summer/holidays, troughs off-season), and
• DIRECTIONAL (full toward the destination at the start of a holiday, empty back — and vice-versa).
Capacity must be sized for the peak, leaving expensive vehicles and infrastructure under-used the rest of the time.
flashcards.explanation: Carriers fight this with charter contracts, dynamic pricing and combining tourist with non-tourist flows.

flashcards.question: Why is it hard to measure exactly how many tourists use a given line?
flashcards.answer: Because tourist flows MIX with non-tourist flows (commuters, business, residents) on the same roads, trains, ships and flights. The same vehicle carries tourists and non-tourists together, so 'tourist transport' cannot be cleanly separated in the statistics.
flashcards.explanation: Stated explicitly for rail in the lectures — it applies to all public/line transport.

flashcards.question: Give the historical chain: which transport innovations triggered tourism growth?
flashcards.answer:
• 19th c. RAILWAYS → first mass leisure travel, seaside/spa resorts.
• 20th c. the CAR/road network → individual mass tourism, motels, road trips.
• Post-1950s mass AIR + CHARTER flights → intercontinental & package mass tourism.
• Today LOW-COST carriers → city breaks, new regional destinations; and CRUISES as an 'industry'.
flashcards.explanation: Each step shows interdependence: a transport breakthrough unlocked a new tourism form.

options: Connector between market & destination, and part of the tourism product itself

options: Each one drives the other (two-way relationship)

quiz.question: A destination with excellent attractions but very POOR accessibility will most likely:

quiz.question: Tourist transport demand is difficult for carriers mainly because it is:
options: Constant and evenly spread all year

quiz.question: The cost of the transport service, within the tourism product, is:
options: Built into the final price the tourist pays

options: Tourist flows mix with non-tourist flows on the same vehicles

options: Mass air/charter flights → intercontinental & package mass tourism

learn.title: Interdependence of Traffic & Tourism
learn.content:
A two-way relationship

Transport and tourism are interdependent: transport enables tourism (it makes destinations accessible and is sometimes the attraction itself), while tourism stimulates transport (strong tourist demand justifies new routes, capacity and infrastructure).

Transport in tourism plays TWO roles:
(1) CONNECTOR — emitting market → destination (accessibility)
(2) PART OF THE TOURISM PRODUCT — the journey is the attraction

Accessibility & price

  • Accessibility — how easily, quickly and cheaply a destination is reached — is a core part of its competitiveness. Poor accessibility keeps even attractive places outside the main flows.
  • The cost of the transport service is built into the price of the tourism product; cheaper transport (low-cost air) enlarges the market of people who can travel.

Why tourist demand is hard to serve

Tourist transport demand is strongly seasonal and directional, and it mixes with non-tourist flows on the same vehicles — so capacity must be sized for the peak and it is hard to measure tourism's exact share. Carriers respond with charter contracts, dynamic pricing and by combining tourist with everyday flows.

The historical chain

Every transport breakthrough unlocked a new tourism form: railways (19th c.) → first mass leisure travel; the car → individual mass tourism; mass air & charter → package/intercontinental tourism; low-cost carriers & cruises → today's city breaks, new regional destinations and cruising "industry".

flashcards.question: What is the dominant PRIMARY form of daily mobility in the EU, and how dominant is it?
flashcards.answer:
The PASSENGER CAR is the dominant primary (1st-choice) form of daily mobility in the EU, followed by walking, public city transport, and (much less) bicycle/scooter.

The car dominates daily mobility in 22 of 28 surveyed countries — highest in Cyprus (~89%), Slovenia (~71%), Iceland (~68%); lowest in Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria (~35–36%). Car share is higher in RURAL areas.
flashcards.explanation: Source: EU Eurobarometer-type mobility survey used in the lecture. The car's dominance is the central fact of EU daily mobility — and the main target of sustainability policy.

flashcards.question: What fuels dominate daily-mobility cars, and how small are the sustainable alternatives?
flashcards.explanation: This gap between fossil dominance and tiny alternative-fuel shares is exactly what the EU Green Deal & Sustainable Mobility Strategy target (see K2).

flashcards.question: What are the MAIN REASONS people choose their primary mode of daily mobility?
flashcards.answer:
Top reasons: COMFORT and SPEED (reduction of travel time), then LACK OF ALTERNATIVE, reliability and satisfaction.

The biggest CHALLENGES of daily mobility are the COST of transport and traffic CONGESTION (congestion is worse in big cities than rural areas).
flashcards.explanation: Lack of alternative is the primary reason mainly in Romania, Bulgaria and Cyprus, and is stronger in rural areas.

flashcards.question: For LONG-DISTANCE travel (>300 km), which modes do EU citizens use most, and who travels more?
flashcards.answer:
Most used for long-distance: PASSENGER CAR, then AIRPLANE, then TRAIN. (>60% of Europeans made a >300 km trip in the prior year; ~40% made none.)

More likely to make such trips: men, under-55s, more educated, employed, those without payment problems, big-city residents, and daily car users.
flashcards.explanation: In Croatia trains are used very little (~1%); the Croatian order of priority is car, bus, plane.

flashcards.question: Are EU citizens willing to switch to MORE SUSTAINABLE transport — and under what conditions?
flashcards.answer:
Yes — in most movements, the majority would switch IF the more sustainable alternative is:
• NOT more expensive than now (price is the #1 prerequisite in 23 countries),
• AVAILABLE/accessible, and
• not slower.
In 24 of 28 states at least half of citizens are ready for such change.
flashcards.explanation: Willingness varies by country (highest in Luxembourg/Netherlands, lowest in Poland/Bulgaria) and is higher among the young, educated, students and city-dwellers.

flashcards.question: Why is mobility behaviour (travel patterns) studied at all in this course?
flashcards.answer:
Because transport DEMAND in tourism is built on everyday mobility patterns: knowing WHO travels, HOW, WHY and WHAT WOULD MAKE THEM SWITCH lets destinations and carriers plan capacity, design offers and steer demand toward sustainable modes.

(The course research assignment has students survey citizens' real mobility patterns.)
flashcards.explanation: The lecture's data come from a large EU mobility survey; the student research task replicates it on a small scale.

flashcards.question: What single innovation do EU citizens consider most useful for the FUTURE of personal mobility?
flashcards.answer: A SINGLE TICKET valid for all forms of mobility/transport in cities (integrated ticketing) — ranked the most useful, ahead of a digital driving licence valid across Europe, and real-time direct payment of tolls/parking/transport costs.
flashcards.explanation: This anticipates the EU 'Mobility as a Service' (MaaS) and integrated-ticketing goals in the Sustainable & Smart Mobility Strategy (K2).

learn.title: Mobility & Travel Patterns
learn.content:
How Europeans actually move

Transport demand in tourism grows out of everyday mobility patterns. A large EU survey (used in this lecture) shows what people choose, why, and what would make them switch.

Daily mobility (1st choice): CAR ≫ walking > public transport > bike/scooter
Car dominates in 22/28 countries · highest Cyprus ~89% · higher in RURAL areas

What drives the choice

  • Reasons to choose a mode: comfort & speed (time), then lack of alternative, reliability, satisfaction.
  • Biggest challenges: cost of transport & congestion (congestion worse in big cities).
  • Fuel reality: ~89% of cars privately owned, overwhelmingly fossil-fuelled; alternatives tiny (electric ~1%, hybrid ~3%, gas ~5%; car-sharing ≤4%).

Long-distance & tourist travel (>300 km)

Over 60% of Europeans took a >300 km trip in the previous year; the order is car → airplane → train. Such trips are more common among men, under-55s, the more educated, the employed, big-city residents and daily car users. In Croatia trains are barely used (~1%); the order is car, bus, plane.

Readiness to go sustainable

In 24 of 28 states at least half of citizens are ready to switch to greener transport — if the alternative is not more expensive (the #1 condition in 23 countries), is available, and is not slower. The most-wanted future innovation is a single ticket for all urban modes (integrated ticketing → "Mobility as a Service").

flashcards.question: What are the BENEFITS and LIMITATIONS of road transport for tourism?
flashcards.answer:
BENEFITS: relatively comfortable, cheap and fast; often NO transfer needed (true door-to-door); tourist experiences possible during the trip; greatest flexibility.

LIMITATIONS: lower safety than rail/air, congestion, environmental impact (emissions, noise), parking/space demands, dependence on road quality.
flashcards.explanation: Road transport is the most elastic mode — its door-to-door flexibility is its decisive advantage in tourism.

flashcards.question: What THREE roles do road vehicles play in tourism, and what are the organisational forms of road traffic?
flashcards.answer:
ROLES: (1) enablers connecting emitting & receptive areas; (2) an integral part of the tourist product (the travel itself); (3) supplying/servicing the destination.

ORGANISATIONAL FORMS (by character): OWN transport · LINE (public) transport · SPECIAL-PURPOSE transport.
flashcards.explanation: The same three-fold scheme (connector / product / supply) reappears for every mode.

flashcards.question: Why is the CAR the central road vehicle in tourism, and which car features matter for travel?
flashcards.answer:
The car is the most numerous road vehicle in tourism — it gives individual, flexible, door-to-door travel between sending and receiving markets.

Key features for travel: efficiency, fuel consumption, SAFETY (active + passive), comfort, speed and emissions.
flashcards.explanation: Active safety prevents accidents; passive safety reduces their consequences (detailed in K2 Safety).

flashcards.question: Describe TOURIST BUSES and their organisational forms.
flashcards.answer:
Tourist buses = comfort, rich equipment, MASS transport. Two basic types: high-floor and double-decker.

ORGANISATION: line transport (intercity), OCCASIONAL transport (agency-organised tourist trips) and SPECIAL transport (closed groups).

Features: large glass surfaces, aerodynamic shape, economical low-emission engines, reinforced cabin (active+passive safety), air-con, AV, toilet (double-deckers: tables, even beds).
flashcards.explanation: City/suburban bus service used by tourists at the destination is a DIFFERENT service from the tourist-bus service.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between CARAVANS and MOTORHOMES (campervans)?
flashcards.answer:
• CARAVAN — has NO own drive; it is equipped for multi-day stay and is functionally ATTACHED to (towed by) a car.
• MOTORHOME (campervan) — has its own drive part + cabin + living space; a self-propelled vehicle for longer journeys with stops, overnight stays, food preparation and tourist facilities.
flashcards.explanation: Both serve camping/touring tourism, letting tourists carry their accommodation with them.

flashcards.question: Compare MOTORCYCLES and BICYCLES as road vehicles in tourism.
flashcards.answer:
• MOTORCYCLE — motor drive on fossil fuel; uses existing infrastructure; smaller parking area than a car.
• BICYCLE — powered by own (human) power; an ecological alternative; needs customised infrastructure; favourable effect on user health and on city quality of life; saves space.
flashcards.explanation: The bicycle is the prime 'active mobility' mode the EU wants to expand (safe bike lanes).

flashcards.question: List the main elements of ROAD TRANSPORT INFRASTRUCTURE.
flashcards.explanation: Passenger terminals and highway service facilities are exactly the points where tourists are present, so they are also tourism-service locations.

flashcards.question: What are the characteristic features of ROAD infrastructure (and how is it financed)?
flashcards.answer:
Big investment, long service life, multi-year construction; method varies by facility type; accurate capacity sizing with reserve; accessibility to all on equal terms; it influences demand on other branches' infrastructure.

FINANCING: as a rule a one-time fee (toll) does NOT cover the real cost → largely state-financed.
flashcards.explanation: These are the general infrastructure features (Category 1) applied to roads specifically.

learn.title: Road Transport between the Demand Market & the Destination
learn.content:
The most flexible mode

Road transport connects the emitting market with the destination with unmatched flexibility — it is relatively cheap, comfortable and fast, and is the only true door-to-door mode (often with no transfer). Its limitations are lower safety, congestion and environmental impact.

Road vehicles in tourism: (1) connect emitting ↔ receptive areas · (2) are part of the trip itself · (3) supply the destination
Organisation by character: OWN · LINE (public) · SPECIAL-PURPOSE

The vehicles

  • Car — the most numerous; individual door-to-door travel. Key features: efficiency, fuel consumption, safety (active + passive), comfort, speed, emissions.
  • Tourist buses — comfort, rich equipment, mass transport; high-floor & double-decker; organised as line, occasional (agency tours) and special (closed groups).
  • Caravans (no own drive, towed) vs motorhomes (self-propelled, living space) — camping/touring tourism.
  • Motorcycle (fossil-fuel, existing infrastructure) vs bicycle (human power, ecological, needs custom infrastructure, health benefits).

Infrastructure

Roads & streets · bridges/tunnels/over- & underpasses · passenger & cargo terminals · parking & garages · highway service facilities · signalling, monitoring & control. Like all transport infrastructure it needs big investment, long construction and is largely state-financed (a single toll rarely covers the real cost). Terminals and service facilities double as tourism-service points.

roadTransportProduct.name: Road Transport as a Tourism Product

flashcards.question: List the tourism PRODUCTS based on road traffic.
flashcards.explanation: Here the road service is the BACKBONE of a tourism product, not just a way to reach the destination.

flashcards.question: What characterises BUS EXCURSIONS and MULTI-DAY bus trips?
flashcards.answer:
• BUS EXCURSIONS — offer spread worldwide; the bus overcomes distance; relatively LOW price; short duration; flexibility in choosing motives; can target the open market or closed groups.
• MULTI-DAY BUS TRIPS — rich, diverse tourist content even during transport; value for money; tourist buses built for longer stays on board; organised by travel agencies; tourist content + transport function combined.
flashcards.explanation: Both turn the bus ride itself into the holiday experience.

flashcards.question: What is PANORAMIC bus transport in the destination, and what else are destination buses used for?
flashcards.answer:
PANORAMIC transport = round-trip sightseeing of natural & cultural sights at the destination; buses with high mobility, manoeuvrability, safety and large glass surfaces; multilingual info during the drive.

Destination buses are also used for TRANSFERS (airport↔hotel, port↔city) and SHUTTLE services (e.g. cruise passengers from port to city, hotel guests to centre) — often part of COMBINED (multimodal) trips.
flashcards.explanation: Combined trips use at least two branches: bus + boat, bus + plane, bus + train.

flashcards.question: What are LOCAL TOURIST LINES and who organises them?
flashcards.answer:
Regular transport within tourist destinations using modest-comfort, low-speed, high-capacity buses.

Organisers: local government, travel agencies, transport companies, hotels.
Purpose: an economical, efficient solution that AVOIDS car use and relieves road infrastructure.
Types: SKI BUS (winter destinations), BEACH BUS (coastal destinations).
flashcards.explanation: Local lines are a sustainability tool at destination level — fewer private cars, less congestion.

flashcards.question: How is RENTAL of road vehicles ('rent-a-car') in the destination organised and charged?
flashcards.answer:
Rental of cars, mopeds/scooters, ATVs (quads) and bicycles via rent-a-car or travel agencies under a RENTAL AGREEMENT.

Payment is either:
• according to DISTANCE travelled, or
• according to DURATION of the lease.

It gives tourists the benefits of car flexibility at the destination without bringing their own car.
flashcards.explanation: Rent-a-car restores door-to-door flexibility to tourists who arrived by an inelastic mode (plane, train, ship).

flashcards.question: Define CYCLING TOURISM and sketch the cycling tourist's profile.
flashcards.answer:
CYCLING TOURISM = leisure travel (day trips or trips with overnight stay, outside the residence) where cycling is the primary/significant part. Forms: one-day, holiday, and active cycling tourism.

PROFILE (ADFC 2020): avg age ~53; earns above-average (~79%); ~50% university degree; mostly without children; 40–60 km/day; ~9-day holiday; 'point-to-point' with accommodation changes; ~29% use e-bikes; focused on quality & experience.
flashcards.explanation: The bicycle is ecological, space-saving and health-positive — a flagship of EU 'active mobility'.

flashcards.question: What does the EU coach (bus) satisfaction survey reveal about WHY people travel by coach?
flashcards.answer:
Most coach trips are domestic (~35% travel to other places in their own country; only ~18% abroad) and infrequent.

Main PURPOSES: visiting family/friends (~34%), holiday (~27%), other leisure (~24%).
Main REASONS: LOW PRICES (~33%) and NOT HAVING A CAR (~27%); then reliability, comfort/cleanliness.
Overall ~64% rate national coach services as 'good'.
flashcards.explanation: Low price and 'no car' dominate — coach is the budget/captive-market mode, very relevant for student & budget tourism.

learn.title: Road Transport in the Form of a Tourism Product
learn.content:
When the road service IS the product

Beyond simply reaching the destination, road transport becomes the backbone of tourism products in which the ride itself delivers the experience.

Road-based tourism products: bus excursions · multi-day bus trips · panoramic/destination transport · local tourist lines · vehicle rental (rent-a-car) · cycling tourism

Bus-based products

  • Excursions (one-day) & multi-day trips — low-priced, flexible, rich on-board tourist content; organised by agencies.
  • Panoramic sightseeing + transfers (airport↔hotel, port↔city) and shuttles — often part of combined (multimodal) trips (bus+boat, bus+plane, bus+train).
  • Local tourist lines (ski bus, beach bus) — economical destination transport that avoids car use and relieves infrastructure (a sustainability tool).

Rental & cycling tourism

Rent-a-car (cars, scooters, quads, bikes) restores door-to-door flexibility to tourists who arrived by plane/train/ship; charged by distance or duration. Cycling tourism — ecological, health-positive; the typical cyclist is ~53, above-average income, university-educated, doing 40–60 km/day on quality-focused trips (~29% on e-bikes).

EU coach survey: most coach trips are domestic and chosen for low price and not having a car; ~64% rate services 'good'.

flashcards.question: What are the CHARACTERISTICS (advantages & disadvantages) of rail traffic?
flashcards.answer:
ADVANTAGES: very large one-time passenger capacity (more than road/air); low exploitation costs; very favourable SAFETY and ENVIRONMENTAL indicators (electric drive, little land use).

DISADVANTAGES: INELASTICITY (line & public organisation; infrastructure-bound); impossibility of door-to-door transport; low commercial speed.
flashcards.explanation: Rail's green & safe profile is exactly why EU policy stimulates a modal shift TO rail (Green Deal, K2).

flashcards.question: Why does the EU strongly promote rail over road, environmentally?
flashcards.answer: Because of its DRIVE TYPE (electric on main lines) and the much smaller LAND/space it needs versus roads, rail has a far less aggressive effect on nature. EU transport policy therefore stimulates rail so it can compete with road and slow road's excessive growth.
flashcards.explanation: Rail is central to the EU's Green Deal goal of a climate-neutral Europe by 2050.

flashcards.question: How are passenger CARRIAGES classified by COMFORT and by PURPOSE?
flashcards.explanation: On a train the LOCOMOTIVE (drive) is separate from the wagons — they can be freely combined, allowing intensive use of locomotives.

flashcards.question: How is rail transport divided by the CHARACTERISTICS of the transport service?
flashcards.explanation: Intermodal/combined transport is how inelastic rail solves the 'door-to-door' last mile.

flashcards.question: What is special about RAILWAY infrastructure compared with road infrastructure?
flashcards.answer:
Unlike roads (built in stages/sections), a RAILWAY CANNOT be built in sections — train movement depends entirely on signalling & safety devices, so the line must be built as a WHOLE. Investor is usually the STATE; the plan derives from the national transport strategy and must fit international corridors.

Road needs only locational compliance at borders; rail needs TECHNICAL, TECHNOLOGICAL and ORGANISATIONAL compliance.
flashcards.explanation: This 'all-or-nothing' nature makes rail investment huge, slow and strongly state-led.

flashcards.question: What are HIGH-SPEED TRAINS (HST), and how energy-efficient is HSR?
flashcards.answer:
HST combine speed (>300 km/h) and efficiency; they reshaped transport by offering a greener alternative to aviation on shorter routes, cutting travel time and promoting economic growth.

Per UIC data, high-speed rail is more than 4× as energy-efficient as driving and nearly 9× more efficient than flying.
Maglev (magnetic levitation) pushes speeds even higher (Shanghai Maglev ~460 km/h).
flashcards.explanation: France pioneered European HSR (Paris–Lyon, 1981, TGV); Germany ICE (1991); Eurostar via the Channel Tunnel (1994).

flashcards.question: What is the function of a railway PASSENGER TERMINAL, and its zones?
flashcards.answer:
A passenger terminal receives & dispatches passengers (and their luggage/post/small cargo), and handles train operations.

Zones of a classic terminal: (1) passenger & baggage reception area; (2) station building; (3) train acceptance zone. Goal: integrate the transport process so distances, waiting and luggage transfer between branches are minimal.
flashcards.explanation: Like road service points, station space is used by tourists → a place to present/promote the destination's offer.

learn.title: Rail Transport between the Demand Market & the Destination
learn.content:
The green, high-capacity mode

Rail offers very large capacity, low operating costs and excellent safety and environmental indicators (electric drive, little land use). Its price is inelasticity — it is bound to fixed lines and public/line organisation, cannot do door-to-door, and has low commercial speed.

Rail = large capacity + low cost + safe + GREEN  BUT  inelastic + no door-to-door + slow
HSR is >4× more energy-efficient than driving and ~9× more than flying (UIC)

Carriages & service types

  • By comfort: classes (comfort rises with distance). By purpose: local (≤50 km) · mainline · international (most comfort + sleeping/dining cars).
  • By service: urban (city/suburban) · intercity (incl. high-speed) · intermodal (rail + tram/road — solving the last-mile door-to-door problem).
  • Locomotive is separate from wagons → free combination & intensive locomotive use.

Infrastructure, HST & terminals

A railway must be built as a whole (signalling/safety dependence), is hugely expensive and state-led, and must fit international corridors (technical + technological + organisational compliance). High-speed trains (>300 km/h; Maglev faster still) rival aviation on short routes; France pioneered European HSR (TGV, 1981). Passenger terminals (reception · station building · train zone) are also tourism-service points.

railTransportProduct.name: Rail Transport as a Tourism Product

flashcards.question: In which ways is the railway applied IN TOURISM (rail as a tourism product)?
flashcards.explanation: Even when attractive, rail rarely works alone — it usually needs road transport for the door-to-door part.

flashcards.question: What are TOURIST TRAINS (occasional/line system)?
flashcards.answer:
Trains to which special carriages are added — catering, overnight (sleeping) and PASSENGER-CAR transport. Tourist trains connect places over long distances with strong, constant SEASONAL tourist flows.

Car-carrying wagons let tourists keep their own car at the destination — which also reduces the volume of road traffic.
flashcards.explanation: A neat sustainability bonus: putting cars on trains for the long haul cuts road congestion and emissions.

flashcards.question: What is RAILWAY TOURISM (multi-day train journeys)? Give the two styles.
flashcards.answer:
Railway tourism = the train trip itself is the holiday — the transport service DOMINATES the product.

Two styles:
• HISTORICAL / luxury (the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express) — luxury, comfort, fine dining;
• MODERN, landscape-focused (the Rocky Mountaineer) — panoramic coaches, regional cuisine, storytelling, daytime-only with luxury-hotel overnights.
Journeys can cross thousands of km and last 10+ days; have a LINE character.
flashcards.explanation: Here transport is the backbone of the tourist offer — the opposite of rail as a mere connector.

flashcards.question: What is PANORAMIC rail transport in a limited destination area?
flashcards.answer:
Short, closed rail systems in protected nature, amusement parks, caves and destinations, combining high ecological standards with tourism.

Differences from public rail: closed systems of shorter length; non-standard train dimensions; lower speed; capacity & appearance adapted to tourist demand.
flashcards.explanation: Designed for sightseeing inside a destination, not for transport between markets.

flashcards.question: What are railway EXCURSIONS (occasional transport)?
flashcards.explanation: Excursions reuse otherwise obsolete lines for tourism value.

flashcards.question: What are MOUNTAIN RAILWAYS, and how do they relate to FUNICULARS/cable cars?
flashcards.answer:
A MOUNTAIN RAILWAY operates in mountainous terrain — following valleys/tunnels or climbing to a summit; often NARROW-GAUGE for tight curves and lower cost. On steep gradients they use steep-grade technology or operate as FUNICULAR railways.

• FUNICULAR — a cable-hauled railway on rails where two cars counterbalance each other up/down a slope.
• CABLE CAR / aerial cableway — cabins suspended from a cable (no rails) to reach summits/viewpoints.
flashcards.explanation: Funicular & cable-car transport is explicitly a week-7 topic; both are classic destination attractions in mountain/scenic tourism.

flashcards.question: What does the EU survey say about SATISFACTION with passenger rail services?
flashcards.answer:
Most respondents are OCCASIONAL rail travellers (~67%); ~13% frequent, ~20% never. Top trip purpose: other leisure (~35%) and holidays (~23%).

Satisfaction is HIGH for buying tickets (~75%) and timetable information (~74%); lower for WiFi (~41%) and complaint handling (~38%). Most common reason for NOT travelling by train: difficulty getting to the station (~16%). Central/northern/western Europeans are most satisfied.
flashcards.explanation: Many rail trips are INTERMODAL — ~44% reach the station by car/motorbike/taxi.

learn.title: Rail Transport in the Form of a Tourism Product
learn.content:
From connector to attraction

When the rail service stops being a mere connector and becomes the experience, rail turns into a tourism product. It still rarely works alone — road transport usually completes the door-to-door chain.

Rail in tourism: hub→destination links · tourist trains (car-carrying) · railway tourism (multi-day) · panoramic (in-destination) · excursions · mountain railways · funicular & cable car

The products

  • Tourist trains — add catering, sleeping & car-carrying wagons; serve seasonal flows and cut road traffic.
  • Railway tourism (multi-day) — the ride is the holiday; historical/luxury (Orient-Express) vs modern/scenic (Rocky Mountaineer).
  • Panoramic in-destination rail (parks, caves) & excursions (often reusing old lines).
  • Mountain railways (narrow-gauge, steep-grade) → funiculars (counterbalanced cars on rails) & cable cars (cabins on a cable) — classic scenic attractions.

What rail passengers think

~67% are occasional travellers; satisfaction is high for ticket-buying (~75%) & information (~74%), low for WiFi (~41%) & complaints (~38%); the top reason for NOT using trains is difficulty getting to the station (~16%) — which is why ~44% reach stations by car/taxi (intermodality).

flashcards.question: What are the ADVANTAGES of air transport?
flashcards.explanation: Air's unique selling point: speed over long/intercontinental distances no other mode can match.

flashcards.question: What are the DISADVANTAGES of air transport?
flashcards.explanation: The airport-transfer problem means a short/medium flight can take less time than getting to/from the airport.

flashcards.question: Is air traffic only AIRPLANE traffic?
flashcards.explanation: Identifying air traffic only with airplanes does not fully reflect reality, though airplanes dominate.

flashcards.question: Describe air transport INFRASTRUCTURE (the airport).
flashcards.answer:
Infrastructure is needed only at start/end points — AIRPORTS, which are complex multimodal hubs including: runways; manoeuvring areas; aircraft resting areas; flight-safety objects/devices; aircraft-service devices; passenger & cargo reception facilities; surfaces for other modes; access roads.

By purpose: local, national, international airports. Very expensive → built by state/local authorities/airlines.
flashcards.explanation: Airports are located near big cities (the source of demand) but far enough out that the transfer is a real issue.

flashcards.question: Within COMMERCIAL air traffic, contrast LINE (scheduled) carriers — traditional vs LOW-COST.
flashcards.answer:
Line carriers publish a flight schedule and must maintain routes/frequencies. Two camps:
• LARGE TRADITIONAL airlines — long-term dominance, government support, complex systems, agencies, big airports;
• LOW-COST carriers (LCC) — cut prices by: no free food/drinks, max passenger numbers, opening new markets/connecting smaller cities, several flights/day, fast turnarounds, SECONDARY airports, direct online ticket sales, fluctuating (dynamic) prices.
LCC ≠ charter! LCC carry ~30% of ~9 bn annual air passengers.
flashcards.explanation: By choosing small airports, LCC bring tourists to areas outside main streams and create NEW destinations.

flashcards.question: What is CHARTER air transport, and what are its TYPES?
flashcards.answer:
Charter = based on higher aircraft occupancy (80–90%) on high-demand routes, at LOWER service quality & price; needs a CONTRACT between airline (transport function) and travel agency (sales function).

TYPES: (1) WHOLE charter (entire aircraft); (2) PART/split charter (capacity split among agencies); (3) AD HOC (one transport); (4) SERIES (several consecutive); (5) TIME charter (exclusive use for the whole season — most rational/economical).
flashcards.explanation: Charter emerged in the 1950s with the surge of tourist flows; it is the classic 'package-holiday' flight.

flashcards.question: Beyond scheduled & charter: private aircraft, special-needs flights and SPACE TOURISM.
flashcards.answer:
• PRIVATE aircraft — symbolic market share; greater mobility/flexibility; company or individual owned.
• SPECIAL-NEEDS small-aircraft flights in a destination — panoramic (sightseeing), photography/filming/nature, sports/recreation (skydiving; + paragliding/hang-gliding without aircraft).
• SPACE TOURISM (since 2000): orbital, suborbital, lunar; first space tourist Dennis Tito (2001, ISS, ~$20 m); spaceflight's carbon footprint is ~100× a long-haul flight; demand exceeds supply despite high prices.
flashcards.explanation: Companies: Blue Origin (Bezos), Virgin Galactic (Branson) — suborbital tourist flights since July 2021.

Choosing secondary/smaller airports and connecting smaller cities

learn.title: Air Transport (Connecting & Tourism Product)
learn.content:
Speed over distance

Air transport dominates intercontinental passenger and tourist flows. Its unbeatable edge is speed (~900 km/h) over long distances, with infrastructure needed only at the airports (routes are imagined corridors).

+ speed · long distance · no route infrastructure  |  − inelastic · airport-transfer problem · high fuel & cost · modest capacity (~500 pax)

Commercial air traffic

  • Line (scheduled): large traditional airlines vs low-cost carriers (LCC) — LCC cut cost via no frills, secondary airports, fast turnarounds, online sales, dynamic pricing; LCC ≠ charter; LCC carry ~30% of ~9 bn annual air passengers and create new destinations.
  • Charter: high occupancy (80–90%), lower quality/price, by contract (airline = transport, agency = sales). Types: whole · part/split · ad hoc · series · time (whole season, most economical).
  • Private aircraft, special-needs small-aircraft flights (panoramic, sports/skydiving) and space tourism (orbital/suborbital/lunar; first tourist Dennis Tito, 2001; ~100× the carbon footprint of a long-haul flight).

Air ≠ airplane only

Airplanes dominate, but balloons (economical, less safe) and historic zeppelins (transoceanic airships) are also air carriers. Airports are complex, expensive multimodal hubs near big cities — but far enough out that the transfer can take longer than a short flight.

flashcards.question: What is the role of MARITIME passenger transport today, and the SHIP's characteristics?
flashcards.answer:
Once the most important branch, maritime now has a MODEST share of passenger flows (its cargo role remains irreplaceable). Passenger maritime is limited to line service over shorter distances, round trips/excursions and personal-needs transport.

SHIP characteristics: large capacity; LOW speed; low transport costs; route flexibility (no route infrastructure); the second-safest means of transport (after rail).
flashcards.explanation: Like air, ships need no built route — only ports — but they are slow, so passenger use is mostly tourism/local lines.

flashcards.question: Compare HIGH-SPEED SHIPS and FERRIES.
flashcards.answer:
• HIGH-SPEED SHIPS (catamarans, hydrofoils) — light materials, gas-turbine/jet propulsion, high speeds; smaller one-time capacity → sail several times a day; economical only on high-constant-demand lines.
• FERRIES — carry passengers AND vehicles; need very SHORT port stays (organised like airports) for many turnovers = large 'dynamic' capacity; biggest ones resemble cruise ships (cabins, entertainment).
flashcards.explanation: Ferries trade comfort for throughput; high-speed ships trade capacity for speed.

flashcards.question: Describe maritime transport INFRASTRUCTURE (ports, terminals, marinas).
flashcards.answer:
Ports → specialised passenger TERMINALS (reception of ships & passengers, comfort, links to other modes). Types: terminals for regular line traffic; for round trips in territorial sea; for INTERNATIONAL cruises (near airport, police/customs, rich facilities). The key element is the WHARF (pier).

Also: MARINAS, sports ports & harbours (the basis of nautical tourism), and signalling/safety devices & waterways.
flashcards.explanation: International cruise terminals double as part of the tourist product — designed so waiting feels like part of the cruise.

flashcards.question: How is maritime transport ORGANISED, and what defines LINE passenger traffic?
flashcards.answer:
Organisation: (A) LINE traffic; (B) SPECIAL-NEEDS traffic (round trips & excursions — exclusively tourism); (C) PERSONAL-needs traffic.

LINE traffic runs by a sailing schedule (seasonal), maintained by a group of similar ships, operated by a liner shipping company — on high-demand lines (private/state) AND low-demand 'lines of special state interest' (state-subsidised, e.g. to sustain island life & tourism).
flashcards.explanation: State subsidies on unprofitable island lines keep both island life and island tourism possible.

flashcards.question: Contrast INTERNATIONAL CRUISES with cruises in territorial waters.
flashcards.answer:
• INTERNATIONAL cruises — huge CRUISE SHIPS (thousands of pax; largest ~7,600 on 'Icon of the Seas'), 20 decks, many facilities; profit via ECONOMIES OF SCALE; ~1/3 of passenger numbers are 'white staff'; tourist product = transport + on-board offer + ports visited.
• TERRITORIAL-water cruises — smaller ships (≤~150 pax), simpler organisation, smaller ports/destinations, offer built on local gastronomy, sea & nature.
flashcards.explanation: Cruise revenue is forecast in the tens of billions of USD; the most popular regions are the Caribbean and the Mediterranean.

flashcards.question: What is NAUTICAL TOURISM, and how is its transport function realised?
flashcards.answer:
Nautical tourism = sailing & staying in special vessels (boats/yachts, rented or owned) for recreation, sport and leisure — a tourism form based on the transport component of maritime transport. Needs accessible, indented, warm, moderate-climate coasts.

Transport function via: (a) PORT-NAUTICAL activity in MARINAS (infrastructure), and (b) RENTING/CHARTERING a vessel (daily, weekly, local, international charter).
flashcards.explanation: Marinas (commercial/club/sports) are the backbone; charter (with or without skipper) is the rental side.

flashcards.question: What characterises INLAND WATERWAY (river-lake-canal) transport in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
INLAND WATER = river + canal + lake traffic. Features: route inelasticity, low speed, high dependence on WEATHER & water level, unequal river characteristics, costly waterway maintenance.

Role in tourism is SMALL but with niches: river CRUISES (smaller ships, ~up to 400 pax, continuous bank views — chosen by those who fear rough seas) and EXCURSIONS/panoramic trips. Famous rivers: Nile, Rhine, Danube, Yangtze, Mississippi.
flashcards.explanation: River cruising suits travellers who want calm water and constant scenery rather than open-sea sailing.

options: Carries passengers AND vehicles, with very short port stays for many turnovers

quiz.question: International cruise ships base their profitability on:

options: Sustain island life and enable tourism where transport would otherwise be unprofitable

quiz.question: The backbone infrastructure of nautical tourism is the:
Compared with maritime cruises, river cruises typically have:
options: Far larger ships and rough water

learn.title: Water Transport — Maritime & Inland Waterway
learn.content:
Slow, spacious, scenic

Water transport needs no built route (only ports), offers huge capacity and low cost, but is slow. The ship is the second-safest mode (after rail). In passenger flows its role is modest and largely touristic.

Maritime organisation: (A) LINE · (B) SPECIAL-NEEDS (round trips & excursions = tourism) · (C) PERSONAL
Vessels: high-speed ships (speed) · ferries (passengers + vehicles, throughput) · cruise ships (scale)

Cruises & nautical tourism

  • International cruises — giant ships (largest ~7,600 pax, 'Icon of the Seas'), profit via economies of scale; product = transport + on-board offer + ports (Caribbean & Mediterranean lead).
  • Territorial-water cruises — smaller ships, local gastronomy & nature.
  • Nautical tourism — sailing/staying in boats & yachts; realised through marinas (commercial/club/sports) + vessel charter (daily/weekly/local/ international).

Infrastructure & inland waterways

Ports become specialised terminals (the wharf/pier is the key element); international cruise terminals are part of the product. State-subsidised 'lines of special interest' sustain island life & tourism. Inland waterway (river-lake-canal) transport plays a small but niche role — river cruises (calm water, constant scenery) on the Nile, Rhine, Danube, Yangtze, Mississippi.

flashcards.question: What determines the VALUE of a transport service to a tourist?
flashcards.answer:
Value = the benefit the tourist gets (being moved, in comfort, safely, on time, with experience) WEIGHED against what they pay (price + time + effort).

Because transport demand is DERIVED, its value is judged by how well it serves the wider tourism purpose — reaching and enjoying the destination — not by the trip in isolation.
flashcards.explanation: This is syllabus learning-outcome 3: place the transport service's value & cost inside the tourism-product price.

flashcards.question: Which QUALITY dimensions define a good passenger transport service?
flashcards.explanation: Surveys show satisfaction is usually high for ticketing/info and lower for WiFi, complaint-handling and disabled assistance.

flashcards.question: How is the PRICE of a transport service built, and how does it sit in the tourism-product price?
flashcards.answer:
Carriers face large FIXED costs (vehicles, infrastructure, crew) and cannot store capacity, so price aims to maximise CAPACITY OCCUPANCY. Hence:
• DYNAMIC pricing (earlier/online = cheaper; price tracks supply/demand);
• the transport cost is then EMBEDDED in the final tourism-product price the tourist pays.
Transport is often a large share of total trip cost, so its price strongly moves tourism demand.
flashcards.explanation: Low-cost carriers and charter are essentially strategies to push occupancy up and unit price down.

flashcards.question: Why is achieving high CAPACITY OCCUPANCY the central economic problem of carriers?
flashcards.answer:
Because the transport service is PERISHABLE (an empty seat is lost forever) and costs are mostly FIXED. A carrier can barely change its fixed/variable costs in the short run, so profitability depends almost entirely on FILLING the capacity on each departure.

Tools: marketing & sales function, dynamic pricing, charter contracts, combining tourist with non-tourist flows.
flashcards.explanation: This is why an 'efficiently organised sales function' is described as essential for airlines and all carriers.

flashcards.question: How does QUALITY differ between, say, a charter flight and a scheduled flight, or a ferry and a cruise?
flashcards.explanation: There is no single 'best' quality — the right level depends on the market segment and the role transport plays in the product.

flashcards.question: What is the role of INFORMATION & passenger rights in transport-service quality?
flashcards.answer: Good, timely INFORMATION (timetables, connections, real-time delay info) and clear PASSENGER RIGHTS (compensation for delays, assistance for reduced mobility, easy complaints) are core quality components. The EU treats integrated information & ticketing and a journey's carbon-footprint info as emerging passenger rights.
flashcards.explanation: Information quality directly shapes perceived value — surveys rank it among the best-rated aspects, while complaint-handling lags.

options: How well it serves the wider tourism purpose, weighed against price/time/effort

quiz.question: The central economic problem of every carrier is to:
options: Maximise capacity occupancy on each departure (the service is perishable)

quiz.question: Dynamic pricing (earlier/online cheaper) exists chiefly to:
options: Fill capacity by tracking the supply–demand relationship

quiz.question: A charter flight typically offers, versus a scheduled flight:
options: Lower quality (comfort/times/airports) at a lower price and high occupancy

quiz.question: Which is a QUALITY dimension of passenger transport confirmed by EU surveys?
Within the tourism-product price, the transport cost is:
options: Embedded, and often a large share that strongly moves demand

learn.title: The Value & Quality of Transportation Services
learn.content:
What the tourist really pays for

The value of a transport service is the benefit (being moved comfortably, safely, on time, with experience) weighed against price, time and effort — and judged by how well it serves the wider tourism purpose (derived demand). This is syllabus learning-outcome 3.

Carrier economics: mostly FIXED costs + PERISHABLE service ⇒ goal = maximise CAPACITY OCCUPANCY
Transport cost ⇒ embedded in the tourism-product PRICE ⇒ strongly moves demand

Quality dimensions (from EU surveys)

  • Safety & feeling of safety · punctuality & reliability · price/value · comfort & cleanliness · frequency & availability · information (real-time/delays) · easy & integrated ticketing · accessibility & complaint handling.
  • Surveys rank ticketing & information highest; WiFi, complaint-handling and disabled assistance lag.

Price, occupancy & quality trade-offs

Because a seat is perishable and costs are fixed, carriers live or die by occupancy — hence dynamic pricing, charter and low-cost models, and an essential sales function. Quality is deliberately traded against price & purpose: charter = lower quality/price/high occupancy; scheduled = higher quality/price; ferry = throughput; cruise = the experience itself. Good information & passenger rights are core quality components.

flashcards.question: How is traffic SAFETY manifested and what does it include?
flashcards.answer:
Safety is manifested through: the number of traffic accidents, the number of dead & injured persons, and material damage.

It includes: the means of transport (freight & passenger), the persons who operate vehicles, and ALL road users. Increasing safety is a CONTINUOUS process and an important determinant of transport-service quality.
flashcards.explanation: Material damage value is not systematically tracked but is estimated at ~1–3% of GDP.

flashcards.question: Distinguish ACTIVE and PASSIVE vehicle safety, with examples.
flashcards.answer:
• ACTIVE safety = features that PREVENT accidents (mitigate the chance): brakes, steering, tyres, lights/signals, vision aids, seat construction, climate control, in-vehicle control/navigation.
• PASSIVE safety = features that REDUCE the damage once an accident happens: body & door construction, SEAT BELTS, headrests, windshields/mirrors, position of engine/tank/battery, bumpers, AIRBAGS.
flashcards.explanation: Mnemonic: ACTIVE = avoid the crash; PASSIVE = protect in the crash.

flashcards.question: What is the 'Safe System' / Vision Zero approach to road safety?
flashcards.answer: Vision Zero's 'Safe Systems Approach' is a PARADIGM SHIFT: ultimate responsibility for road safety moves FROM the individual road user TO those who design and run the transport system. Effort goes into designing roads & vehicles so that crashes do NOT lead to serious consequences — focusing on roads, vehicles and stakeholders, not just individual behaviour.
flashcards.explanation: Strategic frameworks: Valletta Declaration; EU Road Safety Policy Framework 2021–2030; EU target: halve road deaths and serious accidents.

flashcards.question: How do INFRASTRUCTURE and the HUMAN factor affect road safety?
flashcards.answer:
INFRASTRUCTURE: most fatal/serious accidents occur on unclassified roads; fewest on highways & local roads. Infrastructure alone is a factor in ~1% of serious accidents, but combined with a person in as much as ~35%.

HUMAN (driver): behaviour shaped by character/attitude, health condition, and education/culture. The driver is the most common culprit; pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists are most at risk.
flashcards.explanation: Almost 1 in 4 serious speed-related accidents is caused by drivers aged 25 or younger.

flashcards.question: Compare the SAFETY LEVEL across transport sectors.
flashcards.explanation: Road dominates fatalities because it carries the most traffic and is the least 'systemically' controlled.

flashcards.question: What are the key SAFETY features by sector (rail, air, maritime)?
flashcards.answer:
• RAIL — very safe (signalling & line control); fewer but sometimes severe accidents.
• AIR — safety from subsystem elements (communication/navigation, flight control, airports, aircraft) + security against unforeseen events (terrorism: passenger/baggage control, biometrics, explosive-detection dogs).
• MARITIME — passenger shipping adopted the ISM Code (safety procedures); risks: ferry construction (no transverse partitions), high-speed-ship behaviour in rough seas, high automation eroding manual skills.
flashcards.explanation: Each mode's safety system reflects its specific technology and risks.

flashcards.question: Why is traffic safety especially important FROM A TOURISM viewpoint?
flashcards.answer:
Because of the HIGH share of road traffic in tourist flows, tourists are exposed to accident risk — and fatalities/injuries in tourism-heavy countries PEAK during the tourist season.

Responses: information systems for road users (traffic/weather/route info to avoid jams & risky situations) and vehicle-monitoring systems (sensors warning the driver of unexpected behaviour).
flashcards.explanation: Seasonality of travel patterns is clearly visible in the seasonal distribution of road fatalities.

learn.title: Safety in Traffic
learn.content:
A determinant of transport quality

Traffic safety shows up in the number of accidents, casualties and material damage (~1–3% of GDP) and covers vehicles, operators and all road users. Improving it is a continuous process and a core part of transport-service quality.

ACTIVE safety = prevent the crash (brakes, steering, tyres, lights)
PASSIVE safety = reduce the damage (seat belts, airbags, body/door, headrests)

The three influences + Vision Zero

  • Vehicle (active + passive), infrastructure (worst on unclassified roads; a factor with a person in ~35% of serious crashes) and the human/driver (most common culprit; young drivers over-represented in speed crashes).
  • Vision Zero / Safe System — shift responsibility from the individual to system designers; frameworks: Valletta Declaration, EU Road Safety Policy 2021–2030; EU target: halve road deaths.

Safety by sector & in tourism

Safety is lowest in road (and air) — the busiest modes; rail & maritime are comparatively safe (rail ~1.8 deaths/million in 2022; road ~46/million in 2022). Air relies on subsystem safety + security (biometrics, screening); maritime on the ISM Code. From a tourism view, the heavy road share exposes tourists to risk, and fatalities peak in the tourist season — countered by traffic-information and vehicle-monitoring systems.

flashcards.question: How big is transport's environmental footprint in the EU?
flashcards.answer:
Transport is responsible for about a QUARTER (~25%) of the EU's total CO2/greenhouse-gas emissions. Of transport emissions, ~71.7% come from ROAD transport (2019).

Transport is the ONLY major sector where greenhouse-gas emissions have INCREASED over the past three decades.
flashcards.explanation: That 'only sector still rising' fact is why transport is the hardest, highest-priority part of EU climate policy.

flashcards.question: Within road transport, who are the biggest CO2 polluters?
flashcards.answer:
PASSENGER CARS are the major polluter — accounting for ~61% of total CO2 emissions from EU road transport. Road transport overall accounts for about a FIFTH of all EU emissions.

In 2019, most cars used diesel (~67%); electric cars were ~17.8% of newly registered passenger cars (rising fast since 2017).
flashcards.explanation: Because cars dominate both mobility AND emissions, decarbonising cars is the single biggest lever.

flashcards.question: What negative external (environmental) effects does transport cause?
flashcards.explanation: Internalising these costs — making users pay — is a central EU instrument ('polluter pays').

flashcards.question: How do transport MODES compare environmentally?
flashcards.answer:
RAIL is the greenest motorised mode (electric drive, little land use, high efficiency — high-speed rail is ~9× more efficient than flying). WATER is efficient per tonne but slow. ROAD (esp. cars) and AIR are the most carbon-intensive per passenger.

EU policy therefore pushes a MODAL SHIFT from road & air toward rail, public transport, cycling and walking.
flashcards.explanation: Active modes (walking, cycling) and electrified rail are the backbone of 'green mobility'.

flashcards.question: Are ELECTRIC cars really cleaner?
flashcards.answer:
Two ways to cut car CO2: make vehicles more efficient OR change the fuel. Production & disposal of an EV is LESS environmentally friendly than a combustion car, and EV emissions depend on how the electricity is produced.

HOWEVER, using the average European energy mix, EVs are ALREADY cleaner than petrol cars — and will get cleaner as renewable electricity grows.
flashcards.explanation: Whole-life-cycle thinking matters: count production, use AND disposal, not just tailpipe emissions.

flashcards.question: What EU measures target transport emissions?
flashcards.explanation: These tie directly into the Green Deal goal of −90% transport emissions by 2050 (next topic).

learn.title: Ecological Aspects of Transport
learn.content:
Transport's environmental problem

Transport causes about a quarter of EU greenhouse-gas emissions, ~71.7% of them from road. Crucially, it is the only major sector where emissions have risen over three decades — making it the hardest part of EU climate policy.

Transport ≈ 25% of EU GHG · road ≈ 71.7% of transport emissions · cars ≈ 61% of road CO2
Greenest motorised mode = RAIL · dirtiest per passenger = car & air

External effects & the modal hierarchy

  • External effects: CO2 & air pollution, noise, water pollution (tyre microplastics), habitat loss, congestion — borne by society ('external costs').
  • Modal comparison: rail (electric, efficient) is greenest; push a modal shift from road/air to rail, public transport, cycling & walking.
  • Electric cars: dirtier to make/dispose, but with the EU energy mix already cleaner than petrol — and improving as renewables grow (think whole life-cycle).

What the EU is doing

Zero-CO2 new cars by 2035 (−55% by 2030; effective petrol/diesel ban); Emissions Trading extended to road, maritime & revised for aviation; more renewable fuels; end of fossil-fuel tax breaks; 'polluter pays' / 'user pays' internalisation. All feed the Green Deal target of −90% transport emissions by 2050 (see 'Future of transport').

flashcards.question: What is the EU 'Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy' (2020) and its headline goal?
flashcards.answer:
It is the EU Commission's roadmap (COM(2020) 789) to put European transport 'on track for the future' — sustainable, smart and resilient. It identifies 10 FLAGSHIP areas.

Headline goal (Green Deal): a 90% REDUCTION in transport emissions by 2050, on the way to a climate-neutral EU by 2050.
flashcards.explanation: Context: transport = ~5% of EU GDP, ~10 million jobs, but ~25% of EU emissions.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE pillars of the future strategy?
flashcards.explanation: Pillar 1 = cleaner vehicles; Pillar 2 = modal shift & multimodality; Pillar 3 = get the prices right.

flashcards.question: Name key MILESTONES of the strategy (2030 / 2035 / 2050).
flashcards.answer:
By 2030: ≥30 million zero-emission cars on the roads; 100 climate-neutral cities; HIGH-SPEED RAIL traffic DOUBLED; scheduled collective travel <500 km carbon-neutral; large-scale automated mobility; zero-emission vessels market-ready.
By 2035: zero-emission large AIRCRAFT market-ready.
By 2050: nearly all cars/vans/buses & new heavy vehicles zero-emission; rail freight DOUBLED; high-speed rail TRIPLED; TEN-T fully operational.
flashcards.explanation: Notice the central role of rail (double by 2030, triple by 2050) — the modal-shift backbone.

flashcards.question: What does 'SMART' mobility mean (digital/automated future)?
flashcards.explanation: 'Smart' complements 'sustainable': digital tools make the green, multimodal system actually work.

flashcards.question: What is MULTIMODALITY and 'Mobility as a Service' (MaaS) in the future system?
flashcards.answer:
MULTIMODALITY combines the strengths of different modes (speed, cost, reliability) into one efficient journey. MaaS integrates many transport services into one on-demand, digitally accessible service — ideally one SINGLE integrated ticket for a door-to-door, multimodal trip.

Goal: by 2030, seamless multimodal passenger transport via integrated electronic ticketing; paperless freight.
flashcards.explanation: This is exactly the 'single ticket for all modes' that citizens rated most useful (K1, Mobility patterns).

flashcards.question: Give a real example showing how better transport SHIFTS demand toward sustainable modes.
flashcards.answer:
After the Barcelona–Madrid HIGH-SPEED RAIL line opened, the air/rail modal split on that route changed from ~85% plane / 15% train (2008) to ~38% air / 62% rail (2016).

Also: external (environmental) costs of EU transport are ~€388 billion per year — which 'polluter pays' pricing aims to internalise.
flashcards.explanation: When a fast, affordable green alternative exists, travellers switch — proof that infrastructure + pricing can drive the transition.

flashcards.question: What does 'RESILIENT' mobility mean, and why did COVID-19 highlight it?
flashcards.answer:
Resilient mobility = a transport system that keeps functioning through crises (pandemics, energy shocks, supply disruptions). COVID-19 caused steep falls in travel/tourism and severe difficulties for transport SMEs, showing how vital a well-functioning single market and connectivity are.

The strategy aims to help transport — and tourism — 'build back better': greener, smarter, more resilient.
flashcards.explanation: Resilience joins 'sustainable' and 'smart' as the third quality of future EU mobility.

learn.title: The Future of Transport
learn.content:
Sustainable · Smart · Resilient

The EU Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy (2020, COM(2020) 789) is the roadmap for European transport, organised around 10 flagships. Headline goal: a 90% cut in transport emissions by 2050 (transport = ~5% of GDP, ~10 m jobs, but ~25% of emissions).

THREE PILLARS: (1) cleaner modes & fuels · (2) sustainable alternatives in a MULTIMODAL system · (3) right INCENTIVES (carbon pricing, 'polluter pays')

Milestones

  • 2030: ≥30 m zero-emission cars · 100 climate-neutral cities · HSR doubled · collective travel <500 km carbon-neutral · large-scale automated mobility.
  • 2035: zero-emission large aircraft market-ready.
  • 2050: nearly all road vehicles zero-emission · rail freight doubled · HSR tripled · TEN-T complete.

Smart & resilient

Smart: connected/automated mobility (CCAM), Mobility as a Service (one integrated ticket), AI, 5G, a Common Mobility Data Space, ERTMS (rail) & Single European Sky (air), drones. Resilient: a system that survives crises — COVID-19 showed how vital connectivity is for transport and tourism. Proof it works: after Barcelona–Madrid HSR opened, the air/rail split moved from 85/15 (2008) to 38/62 in favour of rail (2016); EU transport's external costs (~€388 bn/yr) are what pricing aims to internalise.

flashcards.question: Which topics make up the two midterm 'halves' that the final combines?
flashcards.answer:
1st midterm (weeks 1–6): Theoretical basis of traffic · Interdependence of traffic & tourism · Mobility & travel patterns · Road transport ↔ destination · Road transport as a tourism product · Rail transport ↔ destination.

2nd midterm (weeks 7–15): Rail as a tourism product (+ funicular/cable car) · Air transport · Water transport · Value & quality of services · Safety in traffic · Ecological aspects · The future of transport.
flashcards.explanation: K1 = theory + road + rail-connector; K2 = the remaining modes + services, safety, ecology & future.

flashcards.question: CROSS-TOPIC: for EVERY mode the lectures use the same two-role scheme — what is it?
flashcards.answer:
Each transport mode is treated (1) BETWEEN the demand market and the destination (its role as a CONNECTOR — accessibility), and (2) IN THE FORM OF A TOURISM PRODUCT (when the journey itself is the attraction).

Road: connector vs bus tours/cycling. Rail: connector vs railway tourism. Air: connector vs charter/space. Water: connector vs cruises/nautical.
flashcards.explanation: Spotting this pattern is the single best way to organise the whole course in your head.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: rank the modes on SPEED, COST, SAFETY, ECOLOGY and ELASTICITY.
flashcards.answer:
• SPEED: air ≫ (HS) rail > road > water.
• COST per passenger: water/rail low · road medium · air high.
• SAFETY: rail safest, then maritime; ROAD & AIR least safe (most traffic).
• ECOLOGY: rail greenest (electric); car & air most carbon-intensive.
• ELASTICITY: road most elastic (door-to-door); rail/air/water inelastic (line/infrastructure-bound).
flashcards.explanation: No mode wins on everything — which is exactly why tourist transport is multimodal.

flashcards.question: CROSS-TOPIC: where does 'INELASTICITY' appear, and why does it force MULTIMODALITY?
flashcards.answer: Rail, air and water are INELASTIC — bound to lines, airports, ports and schedules, and cannot do door-to-door. So they need ROAD transport (transfers, shuttles, rent-a-car, car-carrying trains) to complete the journey → tourist transport is typically MULTIMODAL (combined trips: bus+plane, bus+boat, bus+train).
flashcards.explanation: Road's elasticity is the glue that connects all the inelastic modes to the door.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: how do SAFETY (active/passive) and ECOLOGY tie into transport-service QUALITY & policy?
flashcards.answer:
• Safety: ACTIVE (prevent crash) + PASSIVE (reduce damage); safety is a QUALITY dimension and is lowest in road/air.
• Ecology: transport ≈ 25% of EU emissions (road ≈ 71.7%, cars ≈ 61% of road CO2); the only sector still rising.
• Both are steered by TRANSPORT POLICY — 'polluter pays' pricing, modal shift to rail, the Green Deal's −90% by 2050.
flashcards.explanation: Quality, safety, ecology and policy are the 'why it matters' layer over the modes.

flashcards.question: CROSS-TOPIC: trace the SUSTAINABILITY thread from daily mobility to the EU future strategy.
flashcards.answer: Daily mobility = car-dominated & fossil-fuelled (patterns), but citizens will switch IF a green alternative is affordable, available & not slower → EU pushes a MODAL SHIFT to rail/public/active transport, integrated ticketing (MaaS), zero-emission vehicles & carbon pricing → goal: −90% transport emissions by 2050 (Sustainable & Smart Mobility Strategy).
flashcards.explanation: The course builds from how people move now to how the EU wants them to move in future.

flashcards.question: EXAM REVIEW: match each tourism product to its mode — cruise, charter, railway tourism, rent-a-car, nautical tourism, funicular.
flashcards.answer:
• CRUISE & NAUTICAL TOURISM → WATER (maritime).
• CHARTER (and space tourism) → AIR.
• RAILWAY TOURISM & FUNICULAR/cable car → RAIL.
• RENT-A-CAR, bus excursions & cycling tourism → ROAD.

In each, the transport service is the BACKBONE of the tourism product.
flashcards.explanation: These are the classic 'transport as a tourism product' examples per mode.
